items.title: How AI Agents Work: Connectors, MCP & Agent Safety | Stanford CS193T Lecture 5 with Cynthia Bailey
items.summary:
Explore AI courses and programs from Stanford Online: https://stanford.io/4BYTekh 

What happens when AI stops just writing and starts acting on your behalf? In this Stanford CS193T: Thinking with AI lecture recording, Senior Lecturer Cynthia Bailey explains how AI agents work and why prompt injection gets much worse once AI can take actions. She opens with connectors, the links that let AI read your email, calendar, or files and act on your behalf, and shows that nothing new is happening inside the model: it's the same next-token prediction behind every chatbot, occasionally generating specially structured text that triggers actions. From there she builds the vocabulary for autonomous work: the analyze, act, observe loop every agent runs on, the seven-part "anatomy" of a well-specified agent, and professional-grade agentic workflow techniques like "the elephant and the goldfish." The lecture closes by putting on a pessimistic security hat: for any agent you design, what's the worst that could happen, and whose permissions made it possible?

Key questions answered in this lecture recording:
Q: What is the difference between generative AI and agentic AI?
A: Bailey says agentic AI focuses on taking actions rather than only generating content, but it runs on the same next-token prediction: the LLM emits structured JSON text that a connector turns into an action.

Q: What is an AI connector?
A: Connectors are access permissions that plug your AI tool into apps like Gmail or Outlook so it can pull in data or act on your behalf. Enabling one adds tool instructions to the context window, using the Model Context Protocol (MCP).

Q: What should you include when you define an AI agent?
A: Bailey treats an agent spec as a detailed scope of work with seven parts: goal, context, tools, permissions, memory, actions, and stopping conditions. Stopping conditions matter because agents keep going until told to stop.

Q: What is the elephant and the goldfish method for AI agents?
A: The elephant is a long interview-me chat that produces a 4 to 6 page scope of work. A fresh, memoryless goldfish reads only that document and reports whether agents could execute it without clarifying questions; repeat until no goldfish has questions.

Q: What does human in the loop mean in AI agents?
A: It describes where in the agent loop a human is informed and can approve or block progress. Bailey argues the degree of human in the loop is the main difference between plain chat, connectors, and fully autonomous agents.

Q: How do you make AI agents safer?
A: Bailey urges a "what's the worst that could happen" mindset and least privilege access: give agents only the permissions the task needs. She also flags prompt injection and adding human approval before irreversible actions like permanent deletes.

About the speaker:
Cynthia Bailey is a Senior Lecturer in the Computer Science Department at Stanford University. In 2023-2024, she served as an AI Policy Fellow in the United States Senate through the American Association for the Advancement of Science (AAAS). Her scholarship focuses on computer science education, AI/machine learning, and the social impacts of technology, including creating courses such as Equity and Governance for Artificial Intelligence and Race and Gender in Silicon Valley. Her teaching and research awards include the Lloyd W. Dinkelspiel Award for exceptional contributions to undergraduate education at Stanford, the Lasting Impact Award from the International Computing Education Research conference, a "Top 10 Papers of All Time" award at the 50th anniversary of the ACM SIGCSE Technical Symposium, and the Stanford Society of Women Engineers' Professor of the Year. She has consulted for Apple, NASA, law firms, and machine learning startups. She holds a Ph.D. in Computer Science from UC San Diego.

items.title: NVIDIA DGX Spark Developer Kit Turns a Desk Into a Supercomputing Lab
items.summary: At SC26, an annual supercomputing conference taking place this week in Chicago, NVIDIA is introducing the DGX Spark HPC Developer Kit for researchers, academics and developers. items.content:
At SC26, an annual supercomputing conference taking place this week in Chicago, NVIDIA is introducing the DGX Spark HPC Developer Kit for researchers, academics and developers.

The kit is a four-node cluster of NVIDIA DGX Spark systems, each connected directly to its two neighbors in a ring, with an NVIDIA HPC SDK installation playbook coming soon. Researchers get a place at their desk to run multi-node scientific workloads, AI models and agents, instead of waiting for time on a shared GPU cluster. The kit puts the GB10 Grace Blackwell Superchip on researchers’ desks. 

A Supercomputing Lab on Any Desk

The DGX Spark Developer Kit changes how researchers work.

 

Read All NVIDIA Announcements From SC26

 

It scales from one system, or node, to four — linked directly to one another over NVIDIA ConnectX-7 networking, with no network switch to buy or set up. 

At four nodes, it provides 512GB of combined memory and 20TB of NVMe storage that provides researchers more capacity to distribute models and scientific workloads across the cluster. With NVFP4, researchers can deploy models with up to 700B parameters locally across the four DGX Spark clusters, such as DeepSeek V4.1.

With that much power at the desk, researchers with a fixed compute and server allocation no longer have to wait in a queue for every job. Teams can develop and debug on their own, saving server hours for production runs and keeping unpublished results, and proprietary datasets on premises.

The playbook for NVIDIA HPC SDK is coming soon, bringing GPU-accelerated C, C++ and Fortran compilers, libraries and message passing interface tools to the DGX Spark cluster — the same development tools used on NVIDIA-powered supercomputers. Teams can build and test scientific applications across four nodes, check how computation and data are distributed, and debug communication issues before scaling to larger systems.

The kit brings scientific simulation and AI models and agents to the desktop, with demonstrated four-system workloads including LAMMPS with Kokkos for materials simulation and NAMD for molecular dynamics. The broader DGX Spark community has validated GROMACS for molecular dynamics, OpenFOAM for fluid dynamics, WRF for weather modeling and NVIDIA NIM microservices such as OpenFold3 and Boltz-2 for predicting biomolecular structures.

Running on DGX Spark, new open dataset and post-training recipes for Nemotron 3.5 Super VL help researchers adapt the model for life sciences and chemistry, enabling secure scientific workflows on infrastructure organizations control.

What Researchers Can Do With It

The kit opens up new possibilities for researchers. 

Researchers can explore agent-assisted workflows that prepare simulation inputs, launch runs and summarize results, while the scientists validate the setup and conclusions.  

Researchers can also train AI models that approximate slow simulations, then use them to refine wing designs toward minimum drag. 

Before committing supercomputer time, a team can narrow a 10-million-cell simulation to the 50-500 dimensions that matter.

  • Kvantify is using NVIDIA cuQuantum, and reports running tensor-network simulations of quantum-chemistry circuits with up to 70 qubits and 975 gates on a single DGX Spark, benchmarking circuits generated for penicillin ground-state energy calculations.
  • CYRAN AI, an IIT Delhi spin-out, uses DGX Spark and its PixelFlux library to accelerate JPEG 2000 decoding for large satellite images, supporting local geospatial analysis.
  • OpenFold shows how researchers can fine-tune OpenFold3 on NVIDIA DGX Spark to improve protein-ligand structure predictions for drug discovery.
  • The Rubin Lab at IGI at University of California, Berkeley is using a DGX Spark and NVIDIA Evo 2 model to predict bacterial traits directly from genome sequences by comparing embeddings from genomic and protein language models against the classical baselines. With no 11-hour cluster queue times, results arrived 15x sooner on DGX Spark.
  • The Hartwig Group at UC Berkeley is using a DGX Spark to perform LoRA fine-tuning on the Nemotron 3 Super 120B-A12B model for chemistry machine learning, training a prediction head on experimental values. By running locally on the Spark using NVFP4 quantization, the lab successfully fit a 120B-class model on a single device and bypassed multi-day cluster queue times, allowing them to run continuous eight- to 24-hour training fits back-to-back.

Where to Find the Kit

The developer kit is on display at SC26 and available for sale. DGX Spark products and cables can be purchased from top OEM partners and are also available through NVIDIA Marketplace. 

Partners include Acer, ASUS, Dell Technologies, GIGABYTE, H3C, HP, Lenovo, MSI and xFusion.

An NVIDIA playbook for building and running the NVIDIA HPC SDK, a software development kit for scientific computing, is coming soon. Once available, it will give scientists and researchers a local platform to develop multi-node GPU applications, explore FP32 and mixed-precision algorithms and run molecular dynamics and materials simulations using LAMMPS with Kokkos before scaling to data center systems.

Learn more about NVIDIA DGX Spark. 

Subscribe to the NVIDIA Local AI newsletter. Follow NVIDIA RTX Spark on X, Instagram, TikTok and Facebook.

See notice regarding software product information.

What's changed

  • Added support for turning on Code Mode while agent teams are enabled; if you already turned it on, sessions with teams on now start in Code Mode
  • Added a startup warning when an --allowedTools, --disallowedTools or --tools value has an entry that doesn't look like a complete rule
  • Added a message explaining why MCP servers stop loading when an administrator adds managed-mcp.json during a session
  • Added a row to /status that says when your provider or an environment variable such as DISABLE_TELEMETRY turns features off
  • Added a note in /plugin and claude plugin list when a malformed plugin.json field such as author or homepage is ignored
  • Added Ctrl+O to show hidden startup notices
  • Added a hint in the empty prompt that says what to do after a request fails
  • Added an esc to stop footer hint in a subagent's view where Esc would stop it
  • Added OTEL_RESOURCE_INCLUDE_HOST to include host.name and host.id in OpenTelemetry resource attributes (off by default)
  • Added overflowX="scroll" on a mod's Box, and maxLines and wrap="clip" on its Text
  • Fixed cp of a file being refused when only its source was covered by an Edit deny rule
  • Fixed Bash commands that delete or overwrite files (find -delete, cat a > b, sort -o) being summed up in the transcript as a search or a read
  • Fixed a misleading "Dangerous rm operation" warning in the Bash permission prompt on some commands with no rm that Claude Code can't read reliably
  • Fixed background sessions losing the LLM gateway your shell exported after a crash, after a reopen from another folder, or when the background service lacks it: they now stop before any model request
  • Fixed the background service ending your own processes, such as an SSH login, when a process number on its list had been reused by another user's process
  • Fixed rules added in /permissions or at a main-conversation tool prompt, and /add-dir folders, looking saved when the settings file couldn't be written; the terminal now warns and names it
  • Fixed a failed MCP headersHelper, or one not run in an untrusted folder, making other sessions start without that server, for most servers with no stored OAuth refresh token
  • Fixed managed settings with certain key names stopping Claude Code from starting or affecting other managed files
  • Fixed settings files with values nested thousands of levels deep crashing Claude Code or applying only some of the time; values past 64 levels are now dropped with a warning
  • Fixed a settings file saved with an error mid-session being skipped silently; a warning now names the file
  • Fixed the subagent model set in managed settings not applying in Claude Desktop's Code tab; it now overrides your own, as in a terminal, unless those settings also pick a provider or gateway
  • Fixed sandboxed commands failing to start on Linux when the home or config directory is reached through a symlink into /net and sandbox settings deny reads of it
  • Fixed empty placeholder files, including .git/config.lock, sometimes being left in the project on Linux when Claude Code was stopped during a sandboxed command
  • Fixed Up then Enter answering Yes at the folder trust prompt shown under an already trusted parent folder
  • Fixed an extra Enter at the end of setup accepting the offer to make auto mode the default
  • Fixed a message typed over the startup auto mode offer being lost, and its Enter accepting the offer
  • Fixed a note typed on a permission prompt being sent to Claude after Tab had hidden it
  • Fixed PreToolUse hooks in managed settings leaving no OpenTelemetry tool_decision event or permission_denials entry when they refused a direct tool call
  • Fixed letters typed over /sandbox or a delete question in /permissions moving the selection
  • Fixed resumed sessions losing recent turns after a crash when the previous turn ended with an empty reply
  • Fixed resumed sessions losing earlier conversation history when Claude Code ran low on memory
  • Fixed a re-sent file overwriting Claude's changed copy in Remote Control and cloud sessions on Linux with no feature flags loaded: the copy moves to a .kept- folder, or the new file isn't saved
  • Fixed a background session being killed and its request lost when you opened, stopped or removed the older session whose conversation it had resumed
  • Fixed claude purge hiding its prompts when stdout is redirected, where one unseen Enter could delete a project's data; they now show on the terminal
  • Fixed the spend limit menu removing the monthly limit without asking when Backspace and Enter were pressed as it opened
  • Fixed /rewind restoring only some files after running /branch twice while a slow backup copy was still running
  • Fixed /rewind saying "No code changes" when a shell command changed files it can't restore; a turn whose changes weren't tracked now reads "Code changes unknown"
  • Fixed /rewind: Esc now cancels its summary, its list shows more than one past prompt in fullscreen, and a long prompt no longer hides its warning about losing later file changes
  • Fixed Ctrl+C or Ctrl+D twice in /skills quitting Claude Code and dropping changes; it now saves and closes the panel
  • Fixed the usage limit menu erasing your draft and opening while you were typing
  • Fixed pasted text and images being dropped when ↑ recalls a draft cleared with Esc Esc
  • Fixed an edited typed answer to Claude's question sending the old text when you moved on without pressing Enter
  • Fixed going back to a question you answered from its list putting the cursor on the first option, where Enter replaced your answer
  • Fixed /feedback and /bug sending the report when you typed a space on the confirmation screen, and losing the typed report after Ctrl+O or Ctrl+Z
  • Fixed a prompt typed after --add-dir, --allowedTools or another list option being dropped without a message
  • Fixed /plan <description> ignoring the description when plan mode was already on
  • Fixed valid PDFs being dropped from the conversation after the API rejected a different PDF read in the same batch
  • Fixed a session ending after a single failed memory allocation while drawing the screen
  • Fixed compaction on Bedrock, Vertex and Foundry, and with telemetry turned off, sometimes replying to one of your messages instead of summarizing, or leaving Claude's last reply out of the summary
  • Fixed image-heavy sessions on Vertex AI getting stuck on a 400 error about the request size exceeding a 30 MB limit, instead of compacting and retrying
  • Fixed an error when max_tokens exceeded the model's limit: Claude Code now retries the request with the maximum the Anthropic API reports
  • Fixed grep in the Bash tool silently skipping some text files
  • Fixed a crashed Node or Python hook showing only the first line of its stack trace; the error is now shown, and Ctrl+O shows up to 10,000 characters of the output
  • Fixed /goal clear or a new /goal not sticking when typed while Stop hooks were running and background work was still in progress
  • Fixed the automatic session recap being sent after a reply billed to usage credits; /recap still works
  • Fixed auto mode staying on its local classifier, which counts toward usage, because of a stale saved value, such as one from an older Claude Code
  • Fixed "Sign in with your Console account" in /login replacing your Claude subscription login when the browser sign-in used your Claude plan instead of a Console organization
  • Fixed /login ending on "Login successful" while an approved ANTHROPIC_API_KEY was still used; it now says requests still use the key
  • Fixed "Not logged in" staying after turning on the API key in /config; "Not logged in", /login and /status now name an unused ANTHROPIC_API_KEY
  • Fixed claude auth logout leaving credentials behind, and token refresh failing, when only a Console profile's credentials are on a drive that rejects folder timestamps

items.title: How the World’s Most Advanced AI Infrastructure Supply Chain Invents the Future
items.summary: Deb Shoquist leads operations at NVIDIA, overseeing the supply chain and manufacturing behind its AI platforms. That description sums up the job, but it doesn’t begin to encompass what Shoquist has made possible over decades. Shoquist, her team and their global network of manufacturing partners enable NVIDIA to introduce world-leading technologies year-round. Much of the […]
items.content:
Deb Shoquist leads operations at NVIDIA, overseeing the supply chain and manufacturing behind its AI platforms. That description sums up the job, but it doesn’t begin to encompass what Shoquist has made possible over decades.

Shoquist, her team and their global network of manufacturing partners enable NVIDIA to introduce world-leading technologies year-round.

Much of the team’s success comes down to her deep relationships with some of the world’s most accomplished manufacturers, including TSMC, Foxconn, Wistron, SPIL, King Yuan Electronics (KYEC), Unimicron, Lumentum, Coherent and Amkor. TSMC has partnered with NVIDIA since 1998. SPIL and KYEC were assembling and testing its chips more than two decades ago.

For Shoquist, those relationships grow stronger through each challenge solved together on the factory floor, as every generation of technology demands more from the people and tools behind it.

Ask her about the global network she relies on, and she starts with the people. There’s the supplier in Taiwan so eager to get production moving that he calls her at 3 a.m. with a fix to the latest problem. There are the factory workers in Vietnam whose only ask of her are more tools to get more work done. She remembers the partners that supported NVIDIA when it was small, and the work they’ve done to help each other grow.

Shoquist meets with key suppliers quarterly and spends six weeks each year on the road visiting partners in Taiwan, China, Korea, Vietnam and the U.S., where conversations move from meeting rooms to factory floors.

Recently, she paused her travels to accept the 2026 Dr. Lisa Su Woman of Innovation Award — and to share how she finds the right people and companies to imagine and produce at massive scale technology that has never been built before.

Q: How would you describe your job to someone outside NVIDIA?

A: At the most basic level, our job is to convert designs into the physical world. Our design team creates a blueprint, and our job is to transition it into a reliable, high-performance supply chain.

A matchmaker is probably the best analogy. You have to find the partner that matches your ramp style and has the technology that can meet the needs of very precise designs. The supplier has to be financially strong enough to invest in our ramps. They have to be highly technical. And they have to be willing to do something that has never been done before.

If you don’t have all three, you can’t create products at the volume and speed that we need. You need those three legs, and in some cases, if you only have two, you have to invest in the company to make them a partner.

Q: What’s an example of that in practice ?

A: Amphenol’s cable cartridge is the most complex interconnect assembly they have ever built. When I recently visited the Vietnam factory, now in full production, I was struck by the level of precision required to build a product of this complexity.

In this large cable cartridge, there are 1,500 small cable legs. Each one requires a very precise assembly to yield a quality level of less than 1 DPPM, or defect part per million. Amphenol built over a hundred automated lines to produce this product at the speed and scale we require. That takes know-how and technology, but it also takes heart, willingness and dedication.

Creating anything of that complexity and precision with a supplier forges the partnership. The partners NVIDIA maintains are the ones who supported us when we were small, and yet are willing to scale with us today.

Q: What changed as NVIDIA went from selling chips to building systems and platforms?

A: When we were primarily a chip manufacturer, we were small, and the semiconductor industry was at scale. In that environment, it was about picking the best technology match for the products we envisioned.

As we became a data center systems company, we needed more partners. But we’ve also now entered into new technology areas where the scale of the supply base is still developing.

For example, our optical component partners have the technology and the willingness, but they don’t yet have the scale or capital to build fabs for the volume we need. To grow, we needed to support and invest, like we did with Coherent and Lumentum.

Beyond that, with products like CPO (co-packaged optics), we’re creating entirely new supply chains with scale partners that are new to the optics world. Leading the integration of talent across the supply chain is the key to driving this incredible technology to high volume quickly.

Q: You clearly enjoy spending time with supply partners, and in particular on the factory floor. What have you learned there over time that can’t be learned anywhere else?

A: Over 20 years, you meet many individuals key to the success of your supply. You meet not only the CEOs, but also the people that are running the production floor. These are the people that really know the problems of manufacturing.

If you don’t have a tight working relationship with the people deeper in the organization, then it’s hard to have an open dialogue about any challenges. But when you have tight relationships, they want to help you, and they feel comfortable enough telling you, “I need better technical support on the floor. I need more quality engineers. We need a better design. We need to automate this. We need more buffers of material.”

That’s what 20 years of working with our suppliers has taught us. It’s year after year of learning from people, getting to know people deeper in the organization and creating the trust where they can tell us what we need to do to be successful with them.

Q: Demand for NVIDIA technology is already massive and growing. Your job is to make sure NVIDIA’s volume can keep up. How do you make it happen?

A: It goes back to relationships. When you decide that you’re going to push a line hard to increase volume, you have to have the relationships. You have to know their processes in detail. You have to know their people in detail, and they have to trust you. Only then are you in a position to ask them for special favors, because you can do it surgically, and your ask is credible and reasonable.

And when you’re successful together, they’re happy, you’re happy, and the appreciation for the partnership deepens. We all appreciate those that make us successful.

Q: How do you prioritize resources across the supply chain?

A: You need to first understand what the most critical components are, and protect and prioritize production around them. We need wafers like we need air. And the critical component is the TSMC chip. As it comes out of assembly every week, we decide what factory gets what chip.

Every week, we look at factory performance. If a particular factory yield is low, if their time of ownership is not at the level we want, they don’t get more chips that week.

We keep track of every chip, from the identification number on the die all the way to the customer invoice. If you want to be our supplier, you have to support that traceability process. With that process, we took the time it takes from chip out at TSMC to system out at Foxconn and Wistron from five to two weeks when supply and demand requires it.

Think of the supply chain as a large circulatory system with pathways everywhere — and when you need to accelerate any branch of it, you have the power to do that. We have the capability to do that. It’s empowering and exciting.

Q: What’s an example of a time things didn’t go as planned? How did you, the team and your partners find a way forward?

A: We were getting ready to go to volume production with Foxconn and Wistron for the compute board of NVIDIA GB200. The last step in the process was a test managed by an automated handler — a completely new approach for us, developed to meet the demands of high-volume throughput for these complicated products. During the initial ramp, the throughput was significantly below plan.

The operations director of Taiwan manufacturing made the call that to protect the product and shipments, he needed to disable the entire process and return to manual test loading. Our manufacturers backed him without question and brought in the necessary manpower to meet the immediate needs, literally hundreds of operators. That kept production moving, but would not solve the throughput requirement of full production.

As with any operations problem, the root cause had many elements to it: test tray assembly, test tray design, automation hardware design, automation control software, product yield. From all viewpoints, it was a difficult problem to resolve quickly.

That’s when we executed the NVIDIA swarm. Teams from NVIDIA design engineering, operations industrial, and product and test engineering, as well as from Foxconn automation engineering, flooded the line with talent to redesign and reactivate the line before the scale ramp hit.

This is not an unusual occurrence when there is a problem in operations. All teams at NVIDIA are street fighters — action-oriented, and know no organizational boundaries. We say that “the mission is the boss,” but we also live “the mission is the boss.”

Q: What makes this work so exciting for you?

A: Operations is a very empowering place to be at NVIDIA. Our team is designing and implementing changes to the supply chain constantly to meet the strong demand of our new products. The challenges are understandably high, but we’re always given the resources we need to be successful. The only thing between our goals and our success is our own creativity. That is exhilarating.

items.title: From tasks to goals
items.summary:
As agents become more powerful, we’re moving from giving them tasks to giving them goals.

Tasks are:

  • Write this email
  • Draft this blog
  • Fix this bug

Goals are:

  • ‍Reduce my coordination burden while keeping important commitments on track‍
  • Maintain a blog
  • Make this product successful

Under the hood, this move from tasks to goals consists of two more practical shifts:

  • From specifying an action to specifying an outcome
  • From a bounded assignment to an ongoing responsibility

This is changes what an agent does, what it needs, how its built, and we interact with it.

The agent chooses the tasks

Previously, the user would specify tasks. Now, the user specifies a goal, and the agent iterates towards that goal by deconstructing into tasks, doing some of them, updating the task list, etc.

The agent needs to be good at brainstorming and selecting different tasks, which requires new context engineering and prompting strategies. It needs to be somewhat creative - and varied - in brainstorming potential tasks (if it keeps on suggesting the same tasks over and over again, that’s not great).

Practical consideration: you need some way to see what tasks the agent is doing (e.g. a to-do list), as well as prompting for the agent to be creative in coming up with tasks

Tool calls are way less known

When you give an agent task, you largely have an idea of what tools it will call. When you give it a goal - you don’t really know what tools it will call, and you may not even know what tools it will need to call.

E.g.

  • If you ask an agent to send an email (task), you know it needs the gmail tool, maybe a calendar tool.
  • If you ask an agent to reduce my coordination burden while keeping important commitments on track (goal), you don’t know when it will need a email, text, search tool, a browser tool, or possibly other tools.

Practical consideration: you need more controls over what tools an agent can or cannot call

Inbox to ask questions

When you give an agent a task, you’re naturally in the loop. If you don’t provide all the information up front, its easy for the agent to ask follow up questions in chat.

When you give an agent a goal - it may be running in the background and need to get clarification on certain points. It needs a way to ask questions to humans - whether through Slack or a dedicated UI.

Practical consideration: you need a mechanism for a background agent to ask you for clarification

Way to get feedback

The agent needs to know how its doing as it progresses towards a goal. This could either be by checking in on a metric to see if it is improving, or by getting explicit feedback from a human on how its doing. The more closely tied to a metric, the better in some sense (easy for it to track automatically!) but its never wise to blindly optimize a metric, so explicit human feedback may be the best thing. This is why its important to design goals in a way where its easy to give feedback.

You can have both metrics for the agent to drive towards, and a way to get feedback from users. Define how the agent will assess progress, and give people a way to correct its interpretation of success.

Practical consideration: you need to design goals in a way that is aligned with feedback, and also set up a mechanism where the agent gets feedback

Ongoing work needs triggers (and stopping rules)

When you give agents tasks, they run until its completed.

When you give them a goal, they need to work in the background. They are not always running - they wake up at times to do some work. How do they wake up?

Some methods we see:

  • Heartbeats every X minutes
  • Recurring cron
  • One-off cron (reminder)
  • Listening to event stream

That being said, it also needs a way to stop or pause or ignore these triggers. If it gets a heartbeat every thirty minutes, and pings you the same question every time - that’s a terrible UX.

Ongoing responsibility does not mean the agent should always find something to do. Sometimes doing nothing is the right action.

Practical consideration: you need crons and event triggers to wake the agent, and prompting for it to decide when to act.

Memory lets feedback compound

While memory sounds really cool and has captured the imagination of developers for the past few years, in reality it has not been that needed in a task based world (unless you are doing the same task repeatedly).

With individual tasks, the user can supply the relevant context each time. As you delegate an ongoing responsibility, more of that burden shifts to the agent. It needs to carry forward decisions and feedback without requiring you to repeat them.

E.g: rejecting a blog topic should inform future topic selection, not just the current draft.

Practical considerations: The agent needs to retain and use relevant decisions and feedback across runs.

In Conclusion

Giving an agent a goal isn’t simply giving it a bigger prompt. You’re delegating decisions about what work to do and when to do it. Your role shifts from specifying each task to setting direction, defining boundaries, and reviewing progress.

items.title: We rebuilt LangSmith around the agent
items.summary:
Last week we announced our series C and introduced the new LangSmith Agent Platform: a single place to build, run, improve, and govern every agent. With this, agents are now the core object across LangSmith, connecting fragmented workflows for developers and enabling platform teams to manage agents across the business.

In this post, we discuss why we reorganized the product, how the agent model works, what it unlocks, and where we're taking it next.

Why did we rebuild LangSmith?

2026 brought a step change in agent adoption as new harnesses, models, and engineering approaches made it possible to build agents that can reliably perform complex, high value work.

Companies now run many agents across the business: engineering uses coding agents, product is building customer-facing agents, and teams across the organization have various internal productivity agents. These agents are built with different frameworks, hosted on various runtimes, and use a variety of tools and models.

The result is fragmented workflows for both engineers and platform teams.

Engineers work across disconnected surfaces. Tracing, monitoring, and deployments all live in different places. This requires frequent context switching, and in practice results in teams skipping difficult but important steps like building the evals.

AI Platform teams have difficulty answering basic governance questions. Which agents exist, and who owns each of them? What do they cost, and how are they performing? When costs spike, there is often no obvious person to ask what happened.

We wanted to make it simple for teams to manage the entire agent development lifecycle from one place, using any stack, with ownership and governance across all of it.

One platform for the entire agent development lifecycle

LangSmith supports the entire agent development lifecycle: build, run, improve, and govern. Now, we've connected the entire process through a unique agent record.

  • Build: Describe an agent with the new natural language builder in LangSmith Studio, build in code with our open source harnesses, or use any other framework.
  • Run: Deploy on LangSmith Agent Server or keep the agent on the runtime you already use.
  • Improve: Tracing, evals, datasets, annotation, and Engine work on any agent that sends traces to LangSmith.
  • Govern: LangSmith agent registry and LLM Gateway provide org-level visibility and strict controls over every registered agent.

When you open an agent record, its traces, evals, Agent Server, and Engine issues are accessible with one click, so you don’t need to navigate multiple surfaces to find them. Each agent’s local, dev, staging, and production environments sit under the same agent ID, so comparing performance after making changes is simple.

LangSmith is composable, so you can choose the parts you need. If you already run your agent on another platform, you can connect it to LangSmith to improve and govern it without changing any other workflows.

If you build and run on LangSmith, you get more than a single place to manage the lifecycle. LangSmith products build on each other, so you can find, fix, ship, and verify issues in your agents faster. For example, LangSmith Engine can validate a proposed fix against an Agent Server preview before you merge it to production.

The new data model for agents

Before, traces sent to LangSmith used a flat project hierarchy not associated with any particular agent. The traces from a single agent in different environments had no association with each other.

Now there is one agent record, with environments and traces grouped under it. Every stage of the development lifecycle connects to the agent record.

Every agent record includes three properties:

  • Owner: a named person responsible for the agent
  • ID: a globally unique, immutable identifier
  • Type: what kind of agent it is, which determines the information surfaced in its dashboard, its data connections, and evaluation criteria

Evals and governance for different agent types

Different agents do different work, so you need different types of evaluation to govern and improve them. For example, a coding agent is judged by whether the code it writes gets merged, while a customer support agent requires low latency. Agent types build these distinctions into the LangSmith architecture, so each agent record provides useful resources designed around the agent’s goals.

Agent types provide three things:

A data view built around the agent’s work: Each agent type has a tailored dashboard with key statistics and evaluation criteria. For a general purpose agent, this includes a description of the agent, its recent activity, online monitoring, common models and tools it uses, and agent failures surfaced by Engine. For a coding agent, it's merged PRs, token cost, and what type of work the agent completes.

Consistent data without manual setup: The dashboards are intentionally opinionated. When you assign an agent a type, its dashboard is ready to go with no custom views to build first. Every agent of a given type is measured the same way, so when you have three people running coding agents, the measures are comparable across all three.

Data connections: The coding agent type allows you to connect your GitHub repo to track downstream outcomes of agent usage. As we build more agent types, we'll continue to build integrations that enable you to see and act on relevant data for your agents.

We've started with general purpose and coding agents, and we're expanding into additional types for agents that have unique evaluation. For example, voice agents don't just need to solve customer problems, but to interact with customers with low latency and good audio quality. With agent types, we can surface these specific data by default, and make it easier for developers to find failures and fix them.

Govern every agent, wherever it runs

Agent sprawl has become a governance problem, and it comes from three directions. Engineering teams build custom agents. Business units adopt agents from vendor platforms, like ServiceNow for IT and Glean for enterprise search. And employees pick up coding and productivity agents on their own.

Platform teams and AI leaders are accountable for all of them, but asking every team to standardize on one platform isn’t realistic.

With LangSmith, they don’t have to. It works for agents running on any platform that supports OpenTelemetry Protocol (OTLP), including labs and hyper scalers. Connect the agent and it’s registered along with the agents your engineers built, and it’s measured the same way.

Every registered agent has an owner, ID, and type. For admins, this provides a consistent way to monitor and manage the entire agent fleet. Cost and quality metrics roll up to each agent across every environment. If there’s a cost spike from a Glean agent, there is a named owner to contact, along with trace details that indicate what went wrong.

Where LangSmith is going next

The agent record is a new foundation for LangSmith, and we’re excited to keep building on it. With every trace, environment, and deployment pinned to the agent, we can make more workflows simple for developers, with governance built in.

Here’s an idea of what we’re building toward: Engine red teams your agent, finds failures, and monitors for regressions after you ship a fix. Your team reviews production traces in a custom annotation app built around its own review process, and the reviewed examples automatically flow into eval datasets. Trajectories from your best runs become data for fine-tuning a model that lowers cost and improves agent performance. All of it is connected to the same agent record, with KPIs monitored in real time.

Each of these pieces exists in LangSmith today. Now we’re connecting them to make the develop experience even easier.

Also on the roadmap:

More agent types: General purpose and coding agent types are available today, and voice is on the horizon. We’ll keep expanding to enable teams to standardize how they evaluate and govern more kinds of agents, each with the relevant data connections and analytics.

Org level dashboards: Centralized dashboards are available at a workspace-level today. We're working on org level dashboards, so leaders can see aggregated performance metrics and trends across the entire company in one view.

Identity: Every agent already has a unique, immutable ID. Next, you'll be able to register agents in your identity provider so that security teams can manage and audit them like any other identity in your organization.

How to get started with the new LangSmith

The new LangSmith is available globally in cloud, BYOC, and self-hosted environments. You can try it by logging in or signing up today.

The fastest way to get started is by building your first agent with LangSmith Studio or connecting an agent you already run.

items.title: TokenEconomizer: Learning from Experience to Make AI Coding Agents More Efficient
items.summary:
AI coding agents are increasingly help developers fix bugs and build features largely on their own, but every interaction with their models consumes tokens. In each session, an agent sends instructions, tool descriptions, and session history to its model. Most efforts to reduce this cost focus on individual tasks. Yet developers return to the same […]

The post TokenEconomizer: Learning from Experience to Make AI Coding Agents More Efficient appeared first on Microsoft Research.
items.content:
At a glance

  • Developers use AI coding agents in the same codebases day after day, yet agents often start each session from scratch: rediscovering familiar facts, loading unused tools, and repeating unsuccessful approaches.
  • TokenEconomizer is an open-source plugin that learns from an agent’s past sessions in a repository to reduce waste in future sessions, without modifying the agent or its underlying model.
  • Across 277 real bug-fixing tasks, TokenEconomizer reduced costs by 18.4–30.9% across multiple AI coding agents. Costs fell in every repository tested, while task success rates remained broadly stable.

AI coding agents are increasingly help developers fix bugs and build features largely on their own, but every interaction with their models consumes tokens. In each session, an agent sends instructions, tool descriptions, and session history to its model. Most efforts to reduce this cost focus on individual tasks. Yet developers return to the same repositories, giving agents an opportunity to learn from previous work. Without that learning, an agent may repeatedly rediscover how to run tests, load tools it never uses, or spend dozens of turns revisiting the same error. 

In our paper, TokenEconomizer: Experience-Driven Black-Box Cost Control for Coding Agents, we ask a simple question: can experience in a repository help an agent solve future tasks more efficiently? TokenEconomizer, an open-source plugin from UC Berkeley, Microsoft Research, and Microsoft Security, turns completed sessions into guidance for subsequent ones. It reduces waste without changing the agent or its underlying model, so developers can use it alongside the coding agents they already rely on.

Where the tokens go

We first profiled Claude Code on 60 tasks from SWE-Bench, a benchmark of real bug fixes in open-source Python projects, running each repository’s tasks in sequence. Three kinds of waste recurred:

  • Rediscovering the same facts. After a repository had accumulated at least five completed tasks, 30% of tool calls repeated an action from an earlier task in that repository. Only 7% matched an action in another repository’s history.
  • Paying for unused tools. The agent received 23 tool descriptions on every turn, but 16 were never called.
  • Getting stuck on failures. The 17% of tasks that failed accounted for 32% of the spending.

We also tested three popular open-source plugins, each built around a fixed cost-saving strategy. Each lowered costs in some repositories but not others. Together, these findings suggest that effective cost control must adapt to the repository, rather than apply the same strategy everywhere.

Opens in a new tab

How TokenEconomizer works

After each session, TokenEconomizer reads the session’s log and updates what it knows about the repository. It then acts through three mechanisms, using only interfaces the agent already provides, as illustrated in Figure 2.

Micro-skills capture repository-specific knowledge in one-line notes. TokenEconomizer identifies recurring patterns across sessions and proposes corresponding notes. They are added to the agent’s starting context only after several sessions have confirmed the pattern, and retires the note if later evidence contradicts it.

Tool pruning removes tools that repository history suggests the agent is unlikely to use, while always retaining core tools for running commands and editing files. Removed tools can be restored if needed.

Failure-loop intervention watches for an agent that keeps hitting the same failure. A judge model decides whether the agent is truly stuck or still making progress. If it is stuck, the agent gets a short note suggesting a different approach. In the open-source plugin, if the agent is still stuck after the note, TokenEconomizer alerts the developer rather than stopping the work itself.

The controller is designed to revise its decisions as new evidence arrives. Reported savings also account for the cost of TokenEconomizer’s own model calls.

Saving costs in every repository

We evaluated TokenEconomizer on 277 SWE-Bench tasks from six repositories, using five different AI coding agent and model combinations. For each repository, TokenEconomizer started with no prior session history. 

TokenEconomizer lowered the average cost by 18.4–30.9%, as shown in Figure 3, and saved the most in all 30 repository-combination pairs without performance loss. By contrast, lowering the model’s reasoning effort saved similar or larger amounts but led to substantial performance degradation.

Savings grow as experience accumulates. Early tasks can cost more while TokenEconomizer learns, but cumulative costs fell below the default in every repository by the sixth task, shown inFigure 4. Each mechanism contributes savings on its own, and combining all three delivers the largest reduction.

The savings also carried over to sequential web development, with costs 16.0–21.2% lower on Web-Bench. On security auditing, where every task is in a new repository, costs were 6.4–19.6% lower.

Looking ahead

TokenEconomizer opens a path toward coding agents that learn not only how to solve tasks, but also how to spend computation more effectively. Its lightweight controller shows how experience can improve efficiency without changing the underlying agent or model.

The open-source plugin makes these directions accessible to developers and researchers. It is designed to run alongside existing AI coding agents without modifying their underlying models, requires no API key of its own, and keeps what it learns on the developer’s machine. We invite the community to use it as a starting point for exploring agents that become more resourceful with experience, adapting how they work, as well as what they know.

items.title: Lambda Boosts AI Factory Resiliency and Efficiency With NVIDIA Photonics
items.summary: To train an AI model, thousands of GPUs have to work together, requiring a network that’s fast, efficient and resilient. Lambda is tackling the network piece of the puzzle with NVIDIA Photonics co-packaged optics (CPO) switches. The cloud provider is using the switches to connect NVIDIA GB300 NVL72 racks with more than 10,000 GPUs, delivering […]
items.content:
To train an AI model, thousands of GPUs have to work together, requiring a network that’s fast, efficient and resilient.

Lambda is tackling the network piece of the puzzle with NVIDIA Photonics co-packaged optics (CPO) switches. The cloud provider is using the switches to connect NVIDIA GB300 NVL72 racks with more than 10,000 GPUs, delivering lower power, higher resiliency and longer mean time between interruptions (MTBI) to an AI factory at scale.

“Networking has to keep pace with the demands of increasingly large AI clusters,” said Dave Ward, president of cloud services at Lambda. “Bringing co-packaged optics into a deployment of this scale is an important step toward building the infrastructure needed to support the next generation of AI.” 

 

Read All NVIDIA Announcements From SC26

 

In the company’s tests using the switches, network latency — the time needed for moving data — dropped by about 4% at rack scale and by up to about 10% at pod scale. Across rack, scalable unit and pod configurations, the network maintains the same throughput as conventional pluggable optics.

Delivering Power Efficiency and Resiliency at Scale

Improving power efficiency and resiliency matters because the network sits at the center of AI factory productivity. 

In a large training job, one interrupted link can stall thousands of GPUs. With agentic inference, one network disruption can introduce cascading latency effects on many agents. Every interruption costs time, and every watt spent on networking is a watt not available for compute. 

NVIDIA Photonics addresses both power efficiency and resiliency. By replacing pluggable transceivers with co-packaged optical engines on the switch package, it delivers up to 5x better power efficiency and up to 15x higher reliability than conventional pluggable optics. It also uses 4x fewer lasers, which means fewer components that can fail.

Cooler Optics, Replaceable Light Sources Increase Resiliency

Lambda’s deployment uses NVIDIA Photonics switches, each with 144 ports running at 800Gb/s. Liquid cooling carries heat away from the switch chip and optical engines. 

The company reports a median optics temperature of 36°C, compared with 51°C for conventional pluggable optics, and its tests find more stable signal integrity.

NVIDIA Photonics also brings the electrical-to-optical conversion closer to the switch chip. Each switch has 18 removable external light sources, which supply light to the optical engines. Optical engines sit alongside the chip on the same package and convert electrical signals into light that carries data over fiber between parts of the cluster. 

Technicians can replace the light-source modules in the field, unlike traditional pluggable optics, which require replacing the entire module if a laser fails.

Co-packaging shortens the electrical path from inches to millimeters, which reduces signal loss. It also removes the need for retimer chips, cutting both power draw and the number of parts in the signal path.

items.title: NVIDIA Expands Slurm to Bring Quantum Computing Into Supercomputing
items.summary: Quantum processor deployments at supercomputing centers have grown nearly sevenfold over the past five years, with nearly 30 supercomputing centers around the world now in the process of deploying over 50 quantum processors.  Many of these centers use Slurm to run scientific supercomputing workloads, so expanding its support for quantum processors builds on familiar workflows […]
items.content:
Quantum processor deployments at supercomputing centers have grown nearly sevenfold over the past five years, with nearly 30 supercomputing centers around the world now in the process of deploying over 50 quantum processors. 

Many of these centers use Slurm to run scientific supercomputing workloads, so expanding its support for quantum processors builds on familiar workflows and tools, enabling computational chemists, nuclear physicists and materials scientists to bring quantum computing into their research domains without friction.

In a new release, Slurm builds on previous work with IBM, Pasqal and the wider quantum computing community to allow QPU builders to create a single interface to their hardware for every supercomputing center, through a simple file. This makes it easier than ever for HPC centers and QPU builders to integrate and serve their hardware. 

The expansion is already being adopted by Alice & Bob, IBM, IQM, Pasqal, Quantinuum and MQSC and supports the widely used QRMI and QDMI interfaces.

Read All NVIDIA Announcements From SC26

 

Beating the Bottleneck

Until now, integrating a QPU into a supercomputing center meant a new software challenge for every new QPU or supercomputing center. By building on existing quantum-HPC interfaces such as QRMI and QDMI, the Slurm expansion allows QPU builders to reuse their integrations across all their deployments. It also means that supercomputing centers can add new quantum processors to their existing scheduling and resource-management workflows without developing bespoke QPU-specific solutions.

For quantum computing to advance science, it needs to be used by scientists. Now scientists can run quantum-classical applications developed with platforms such as NVIDIA CUDA-Q with Slurm coordinating access to all the processing they need.

Slurm 26.11 will be available later this month. 

Orchestrating Resources in an Open Quantum-GPU Platform

The Slurm expansion adds a community-developed orchestration layer to NVIDIA’s open platform for quantum-GPU supercomputing, which centers around the CUDA-Q open platform for hybrid quantum-classical computing. At SC26, new releases expand all aspects of the platform:

CUDA-Q QEC allows researchers developing quantum error correction to rapidly prototype and test new ideas, including with a new decoder server. A new TCBP-JOBS decoder is 13,000x faster than the industry standard.

CUDA-Q gets an expanded layer of fault-tolerant primitives that application builders can use to realistically compile their ideas. Fermilab has already used CUDA-Q to perform studies in three weeks that would normally have taken five months.

CUDA-Q Algorithms provides reusable components for builders of quantum applications, including new capabilities in helping design the loading data into quantum circuits and tools specifically for chemistry and materials applications

CUDA-Q Pulse gives quantum hardware builders a layer for shaping the ‘pulses’ needed to control qubits on a QPU, including tools to GPU accelerate their generation.

The quantum ecosystem around the world is continuing to build with this platform. Quantum Motion integrated its QUICHE chemistry framework with CUDA-Q. Altera and Oxford Quantum Circuits designed an FPGA-based controller connecting qubit control and readout to GPUs through NVQLink.

At supercomputing scale, QunaSys used cuQuantum and 1,024 NVIDIA Hopper GPUs on ABCI-Q to simulate more than 300 million quantum operations, reaching chemical accuracy for a four-hydrogen-atom model. NVIDIA researchers used JUPITER to simulate 104 qubits under realistic noise, testing fault-tolerant designs before they’re built.

items.title: NVIDIA Sweeps MLPerf Training and Endpoints as Vera Rubin Debuts With Leading Performance
items.summary: In its MLPerf benchmarks debut, with results released today, the NVIDIA Vera Rubin platform delivers leading performance across training, post-training and agentic inference.  NVIDIA swept every MLPerf Training v6.1 benchmark and, in its first MLPerf Endpoints submission, delivered more than 10x generational gains in throughput per watt for agentic AI — measuring how much agentic […]
items.content:
In its MLPerf benchmarks debut, with results released today, the NVIDIA Vera Rubin platform delivers leading performance across training, post-training and agentic inference. 

NVIDIA swept every MLPerf Training v6.1 benchmark and, in its first MLPerf Endpoints submission, delivered more than 10x generational gains in throughput per watt for agentic AI — measuring how much agentic work a system delivers with each watt of power. 

These results are just the beginning. Vera Rubin performance will keep climbing through continuous optimization of NVIDIA’s CUDA-powered software stack, so the infrastructure that customers invest in today delivers more value over time.

NVIDIA Sweeps MLPerf Training v6.1

AI agents are now everywhere, writing code, running business workflows, answering customer questions and, as this week’s SC26 conference highlights, advancing scientific research. 

Faster training means smarter agents can reach users sooner, drug discovery models can keep pace with new lab data and fraud-detection models can adapt to new threats faster.

MLPerf Training measures how fast a system can train a range of AI models to a target level of accuracy. 

The NVIDIA platform was the only one with results on every benchmark this round, spanning large language models, image generation, recommender systems and reinforcement learning post-training. In its debut, Vera Rubin NVL72 delivered up to 2x more performance per GPU than the highly optimized NVIDIA GB300 NVL72 system — early results that show the pace of generation-over-generation innovation. 

NVIDIA also demonstrated performance at scale. On the DeepSeek-V3 benchmark, Vera Rubin NVL72 scaled from 256 to 1,024 GPUs with about 97% efficiency: quadrupling the GPUs cut time to train from 16 minutes to about four. 

NVIDIA also ran the benchmark on 10,240 GPUs with GB300 systems, representing the largest scale in this round. Microsoft Azure matched that scale with 10,240 NVIDIA GPUs with GB200 systems. 

Results at this scale matter because adding GPUs only speeds up training if they can work together efficiently. NVIDIA NVLink scale-up networking connects the GPUs within each system so they act as one, while NVIDIA Quantum-X800 InfiniBand and Spectrum-X Ethernet scale-out networking link those systems across the data center. Combined with optimized software, this keeps thousands of GPUs working in concert, helping developers build more intelligent models while cutting training times.

NVIDIA Vera Rubin Leads Agentic Inference on MLPerf Endpoints

An AI agent for travel that plans and books a whole trip — or an IT agent that finds and fixes a problem before anyone files a ticket — may reason, call tools and check its work many times to finish a single task. 

Each of those steps generates tokens. Because AI data centers are limited by power, the more tokens a system can generate each second for every watt of power, the more agents it can serve and the more value it creates. 

MLPerf Endpoints tests systems on real agentic coding and enterprise workflows, and checks that the agents still complete their tasks correctly. NVIDIA Vera Rubin leads across all of its agentic benchmarks.

For example, in a provisional result for Kimi K3, a large open model built for agentic workflows, Vera Rubin NVL72 systems deliver more than 10x the throughput per watt of NVIDIA GB300 NVL72 at the same response speed. 

Every AI service has to balance serving many users at once against responding quickly to each one. Vera Rubin shifts that entire curve, serving more users while responding faster. 

Leadership Across Benchmarks and Workloads

NVIDIA partners participated extensively in MLPerf Training, with submissions from 20 organizations: ASUS, Azure, Cisco, CoreWeave, Crusoe, Dell Technologies, Firmus, Giga Computing, Google Cloud, HPE, Inventec, Krai, Lambda, Nebius, Oracle, Quanta Cloud Technology (QCT), Supermicro, TTA and the University of Florida. 

Their submissions show how NVIDIA’s programmable platform, with open source libraries and frameworks, lets a vast ecosystem of partners innovate and optimize AI training performance.

The lead extends beyond MLPerf. 

Vera Rubin also delivers leading performance on independent benchmarks including SemiAnalysis AgentX and Artificial Analysis AgentPerf, showcasing how the same NVIDIA infrastructure can productively run everything from pretraining and post-training to agentic inference, as well as workloads beyond AI, such as the high-performance computing showcased at SC26 this week. 

Dive deeper into the results in the MLPerf Training and MLPerf Endpoints technical blogs.

items.title: NVIDIA CUDA-X Libraries Give Agents the Tools to Accelerate Scientific Discovery
items.summary: With expanded NVIDIA CUDA-X libraries, including cuPhoton, cuPotential and cuSpa, researchers can sift through vast amounts of data to accelerate research, from astrophysics and materials science to single-cell biology. The speedups are helping scientists analyze larger datasets and model more complex systems. The new libraries give AI agents the tools to help researchers make discoveries […]
items.content:
With expanded NVIDIA CUDA-X libraries, including cuPhoton, cuPotential and cuSpa, researchers can sift through vast amounts of data to accelerate research, from astrophysics and materials science to single-cell biology.

The speedups are helping scientists analyze larger datasets and model more complex systems.

The new libraries give AI agents the tools to help researchers make discoveries faster than ever.

 

Read All NVIDIA Announcements From SC26

 

Bringing Black Holes Into Focus

Seeing a black hole takes a telescope the size of Earth. The Event Horizon Telescope links radio dishes worldwide, generating petabytes of data that can take months to process.

With NVIDIA cuPhoton.xBeam, a module within the cuPhoton Toolkit, black hole observations from the Event Horizon Telescope can now be correlated orders of magnitude faster than ever. Analysis that once took over a month now takes eight minutes.

By combining global radio dishes into Earth-sized aperture, cuPhoton delivers unprecedented astronomical imaging resolution. cuPhoton successfully correlated observations of powerful black hole jets J1924 and 3C279 in the night sky — making it a reality to reconstruct a Messier 87* black hole galaxy in real time. 

The entire pipeline, from data loading and processing to visualization, runs on distributed multi-GPU systems or a compact NVIDIA DGX Spark system, helping scientists study how gas spirals inward under a black hole’s powerful gravitational pull.

Steering Fusion Simulations

Sustaining plasma at millions of degrees is essential to achieving stable, continuous fusion energy. But simulating its behavior is costly: on petascale systems, a single time step can take days, with simulations running for weeks. Experiments also generate data faster than traditional pipelines can process it, often leaving scientists waiting until experiments end to analyze results.

Pacific Fusion researchers used NVIDIA cuPhoton.xLens module to extract insights while plasma simulations run, helping them visualize what’s happening as results emerge. 

The NVIDIA cuPhoton.xLens module extracts insights while plasma simulations run, helping researchers understand what’s happening as results emerge. Researchers can couple the entire pipeline with an NVIDIA Nemotron-powered agent running locally on the same system, enabling interactive analysis that can help steer simulations in real time to inform fusion reactor target and chamber design.

Exploring Potential Medicines

Molecular simulations help scientists evaluate drug designs before costly laboratory experiments. NVIDIA cuPotential, built on work by researchers at Simons Foundation’s Flatiron Institute and D. E. Shaw Research, accelerates existing simulation software by up to 3x while improving calculation stability and accuracy. It expedites synthetic data creation for generative AI models, finding previously unknown molecular binding sites and calculating the strength of molecular interactions.

NVIDIA is working with Schrödinger and the AMBER, NAMD, GROMACS, LAMMPS and Open Molecular Software Foundation communities to bring cuPotential acceleration to molecular dynamics engines and workflows.

Cadence, Fathom Therapeutics, Topos Bio, Genesis Molecular AI and Terray Therapeutics are adopting it for drug discovery.

Accelerating Materials Research

Daviator, a collection of batched GPU kernels for the widely used Vienna Ab initio Simulation Package, is coming to NVIDIA ALCHEMI — delivering quantum-mechanical calculations up to 22x faster and at up to 75% lower cost. With Daviator, researchers building simulation models can now use GPU acceleration across atomistic systems of all sizes to generate the millions of calculations of atomic interactions needed for model training and inference, including for small systems that previously ran faster on CPUs.

At Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory, the NVIDIA DAQIRI networking library connects a high-speed electron microscopy detector to GPU processing, moving analysis into the experiment itself. Researchers can identify useful signals, discover previously unknown regions of interest and decide what to measure next while measurements are being taken. 

The workflow supports atomic-resolution materials studies that can distinguish elements, laying the groundwork for future automated experiments.

Revealing Biology at Scale

The newly open source cuSpa accelerates cell polygon calculations, enabling developers to generate massive spatial graphs for next-generation patient and cancer models at Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center, with a 900x speedup compared with using CPUs. 

Codeveloped with scverse, the rapids-singlecell framework accelerates single-cell analysis — and is now available in a single, agent-ready container. Using the tool, Therna Biosciences processed data 200x faster for therapeutic design. 10x Genomics integrated rapids-singlecell in its new Sentira platform, helping academic researchers, biopharma teams and foundation model builders accelerate the path from large-scale spatial data to biological insights. 

And the NVIDIA GPU-accelerated HMMER library, also open source, accelerates the annotation of predicted protein sequences, supporting data preparation for biological foundation models. At Basecamp Research, benchmark searches ran up to 84x faster than with standard HMMER, reducing the time required to annotate the large biological datasets used to train the company’s therapeutic design models.

items.title: CUDA at 20: How the Platform Transformed Scientific Computing
items.summary: This week at SC26, NVIDIA is marking two decades of CUDA by honoring the researchers, developers and engineers who helped make GPU computing a foundation for modern science and AI.  CUDA’s 20th anniversary presents an occasion to reflect across computing eras, from the people who wrote the very first CUDA programs to the AI developers […]
items.content:
This week at SC26, NVIDIA is marking two decades of CUDA by honoring the researchers, developers and engineers who helped make GPU computing a foundation for modern science and AI. 

CUDA’s 20th anniversary presents an occasion to reflect across computing eras, from the people who wrote the very first CUDA programs to the AI developers building on their work today. 

At the platform’s core is this developer community whose experiments, tools and persistence expanded what accelerated computing could do.

From SC06 to SC26

NVIDIA announced CUDA in November 2006 and brought it to the scientific community at SC06, giving scientists and developers a familiar, high-level programming model for using GPUs. It fundamentally extended accelerated computing beyond graphics use cases to accelerate demanding applications for science, simulation and more.

In the two decades since, developers have used CUDA to advance Nobel Prize-winning AI research, accelerate scientific applications on supercomputers and support visual effects in Oscar-winning films. 

Today, more than 11 million developers build on CUDA across the computing stack. 

 

Read All NVIDIA Announcements From SC26

 

Honoring the Architects of Progress

Now, at SC26, NVIDIA is looking back at some of the CUDA luminaries who’ve spearheaded breakthroughs in science and AI:

At the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign, biophysicist Klaus Schulten’s team helped connect GPU computing with molecular biology through Nanoscale Molecular Dynamics and Visual Molecular Dynamics, tools for molecular simulation and visualization. In 2013, researchers at Illinois, the University of Pittsburgh and Vanderbilt University used CUDA-accelerated tools to help resolve the HIV capsid’s atomic structure. They combined experiments with simulations on Blue Waters, one of the world’s most powerful supercomputers at the time.

In a critical breakthrough in AI, University of Toronto researchers Alex Krizhevsky, Ilya Sutskever and Geoffrey Hinton used CUDA to train AlexNet on just two NVIDIA GPUs. Their image-recognition system won the 2012 ImageNet competition, helping demonstrate the potential of GPU computing for deep learning. 

That connection between computing and scientific discovery is seen with AlphaFold, which predicts protein structures. Demis Hassabis and John Jumper shared the 2024 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for protein structure prediction. Their team’s publicly released AlphaFold 2 software uses CUDA for GPU execution.

These are just a few of many examples that show how one generation’s work creates opportunities for the next. With 1,000+ NVIDIA CUDA-X libraries, developers are now reshaping industries and giving machines the power to see, learn and reason — from discovering new medicines and designing next-generation factories to advancing autonomous vehicles, modeling financial markets and unlocking quantum computing — and more.

Start building with the CUDA Toolkit and visit the 20-Year CUDA Celebration Event Wall at NVIDIA’s booth at SC26.

items.title: NVIDIA Announces Rubin HPC — A New GPU to Accelerate Agents for Science, Engineering and Analytics
items.summary: Announced today at SC26, NVIDIA Rubin HPC is a new GPU in the NVIDIA Vera Rubin platform designed to accelerate simulation and data processing for science, engineering and analytics workflows.  As agents help scientists and engineers explore more candidate materials, molecules and designs, they rely on simulations to test those ideas and guide their next […]
items.content:
Announced today at SC26, NVIDIA Rubin HPC is a new GPU in the NVIDIA Vera Rubin platform designed to accelerate simulation and data processing for science, engineering and analytics workflows. 

As agents help scientists and engineers explore more candidate materials, molecules and designs, they rely on simulations to test those ideas and guide their next steps. Rubin HPC will accelerate those simulations, shortening the path from exploration to scientific discovery and industrial design.

The Rubin HPC GPU features a record number of CUDA cores — more than 50,000 on a single GPU — as well as a sparse data acceleration capability that keeps those cores fed with data, and accelerates GPU-to-GPU connectivity with seventh-generation NVIDIA NVLink interconnect technology.

 

Read All NVIDIA Announcements From SC26

 

Scientists and engineers rely on simulation to understand complex systems before committing to experiments or physical prototypes. Working with agents, these teams can explore more candidate materials, molecules and designs. This increases demand for the GPU-accelerated simulations needed to evaluate those ideas and guide next steps.

“For agents tackling science and engineering, faster simulation means faster discovery,” said Ian Buck, vice president of hyperscale and high-performance computing at NVIDIA. “Rubin HPC accelerates the simulations agents use to test ideas and guide their next steps, helping scientists and engineers explore more possibilities and bring breakthroughs closer.” 

Turning Faster Computation Into Faster Discovery

Across climate models, engineering simulations, genomic analysis and financial risk, scientific computing workloads take a similar shape: an application reaches into an immense dataset, gathers a handful of scattered values, calculates a result and repeats this on an enormous scale. 

To help address the challenge, Rubin HPC will offer a balanced design, scaling data movement and compute together rather than increasing compute alone. 

That balance is what optimizes Rubin HPC for scientific computing. It keeps the GPU’s record number of CUDA cores supplied with data, so they spend their time computing rather than waiting. This accelerates recurring patterns of every simulation workload — from sparse matrix operations to stencil computations to sorting and reductions. 

These patterns are prevalent across data analytics, science and engineering workloads, which is why a purpose-built GPU delivering the broadest acceleration can help unlock cross-industry breakthroughs.

NVIDIA CUDA-X libraries offer a growing set of optimized implementations of complex algorithms for agents to use, including those most relevant to simulation and analytics. Used together with Rubin HPC, the libraries can give agents the fastest glide path to reasoning outcomes. 

And faster agent-invoked simulations mean faster feedback — shortening the loop of hypothesis, simulation and refinement, so researchers and engineers can choose next steps sooner and point lab work at the most promising candidates.

Rubin HPC is expected to be available in 2028.
